summary: Specifies the Peer-to-Peer Streaming Peer Protocol, which lets peers share the same prerecorded or live audio and video stream among a group. Viewers also help redistribute content, reducing load on the original source.

eli5.summary: Instead of everyone getting the video from one person, viewers pass pieces along to each other, like friends sharing a pizza.

questions: how does peer to peer video streaming work
what is a merkle hash tree in streaming
subtitle: A protocol that lets viewers of a video stream pass pieces of it to each other, with every piece verifiable by a hash.

tldr.problem: Streaming the same audio or video to many viewers from one server is costly, and in a peer-to-peer system a malicious peer could hand out fake content.
tldr.mechanism: Peers handshake over UDP, announce which chunks they have, request chunks from each other and check each one against a Merkle hash tree whose root hash (or a public key, for live streams) names the content.
tldr.outcome: PPSPP is a Proposed Standard that supports on-demand and live streaming, with a short time until playback and protection against tampering by malicious peers.

today: RFC 7574 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC says the format of PPSPP URLs should be defined in an extension document.

sections.title: Purpose and Design Goals
sections.content:
The Peer-to-Peer Streaming Peer Protocol (PPSPP) disseminates the same content to a group of interested parties in a streaming fashion. It handles prerecorded (on-demand) and live audio and video. Clients that consume the content are on equal footing with the servers that first provided it, so everyone can potentially provide upload bandwidth.

The design aims at a short time until playback and at preventing disruption by malicious peers. Content is identified by a single cryptographic hash, the root of a Merkle hash tree computed from the content. Every peer can detect fake content directly, and only a small amount of information is needed to start a download and verify incoming chunks.

PPSPP is generic. It defines a set of messages that can run over UDP, TCP or other transports, and today it runs over UDP using LEDBAT for congestion control. It assumes a peer has already found some initial peers, for example from a tracker. It grew out of research into making BitTorrent suitable for streaming, and most PPSPP messages have a BitTorrent counterpart.
sections.eli5: Viewers share the work of sending the video, so the original server does not get swamped. A single fingerprint of the whole video lets every viewer spot fake pieces.

sections.title: Overall Operation
sections.content:
Messages are packed into datagrams. The RFC walks through three stages. To join a swarm (the group of peers sharing the same content), Peer A learns peer addresses from a tracker and sends a HANDSHAKE to each of them, including the swarm ID. Peers reply with their own HANDSHAKE and HAVE messages that say which chunks they hold. A peer that cannot serve Peer A now also sends CHOKE.

To exchange chunks, Peer A sends REQUEST messages for disjoint sets of chunks to different peers. They answer with DATA plus INTEGRITY messages containing the hashes needed to check each chunk against the trusted swarm ID. Peer A then announces what it now has with HAVE, acknowledges with ACK (not used over a reliable transport) and asks for more.

To leave gracefully, Peer A sends a special HANDSHAKE to its peers and deregisters from the tracker. If a peer crashes, others drop it when it stops sending messages.

There are no error codes. Invalid messages are discarded and further communication with that peer should stop. A good peer is one that responds with chunks, and the content is available from many sources, so a peer need not try hard with any one of them.
sections.eli5: You tell a few neighbors what video you want, they tell you which pieces they have, and you swap pieces. If a neighbor goes quiet, you just ask someone else.

sections.title: Handshake, Channels and Keep-Alives
sections.content:
To talk to Peer Q about Swarm S, Peer P needs the swarm metadata: swarm ID, chunk size, chunk addressing method, integrity protection method, and the Merkle hash function if applicable. The first datagram P sends MUST start with a HANDSHAKE, carry a randomly chosen channel ID, and be prefixed with destination channel ID 0. It may carry minor payload such as HAVE messages but MUST NOT carry a heavy payload such as DATA.

If Q is in the same swarm and interested, it replies with its own HANDSHAKE and channel ID, in a datagram prefixed with P's channel ID. If any check fails, Q MUST NOT reply, because the first datagram may have been spoofed. Once P sees its own channel ID echoed, P knows Q really responds and may start sending heavy payload. Once Q sees a datagram with its own channel ID, the three-way handshake is complete. A peer closes a channel with a HANDSHAKE carrying an all-zeros channel ID.

Channels let several swarms share one transport address, which matters because of NATs and firewalls. Each channel belongs to one swarm, and each end uses a different random ID for it. A peer SHOULD send keep-alives to peers it is interested in. Over UDP, a peer is declared dead after a three minute delay since the last packet from it and at least three datagrams sent to it in the same period. Keep-alives are simple datagrams consisting only of a four-byte channel ID.
sections.eli5: Before swapping pieces, two peers trade secret ticket numbers so each knows the other is really there and not someone pretending. Short check-in notes keep the line open.

sections.title: The Messages
sections.content:
Over UDP the first byte of each message gives its type, and integers are big-endian. Key messages:

  • HAVE announces chunks a peer has verified. Withholding it works as a form of choking.
  • REQUEST asks for chunks, and CANCEL withdraws a request. Receiving a HAVE for the chunk acts as an implicit cancel. Live swarms may also push data without requests.
  • DATA carries a chunk, plus a timestamp because LEDBAT needs one. A DATA message in a datagram goes at the tail.
  • ACK must be sent over unreliable transports and carries a one-way delay sample.
  • INTEGRITY and SIGNED_INTEGRITY carry hashes and signatures needed to verify chunks.
  • CHOKE says the sender will no longer answer requests, and UNCHOKE says it will again. Both are informational, since answering requests is optional.

The peer-exchange messages PEX_REQ and PEX_RES* let peers share addresses, reducing the need for a tracker. This is optional, and the RFC warns it enables attacks, so it should not be used on the Internet without extra measures. PEX_REScert carries a signed swarm-membership certificate. PEX_RESv4 and PEX_RESv6 carry bare addresses and MUST only be used in benign environments such as private networks.

All messages are idempotent or recognizable as duplicates, so a peer may resend them when it suspects loss.
sections.eli5: The messages are like a small set of phrases: "I have these pieces", "please send piece 5", "here it is", "got it", "I am too busy right now".

sections.title: Chunk Addressing
sections.content:
A chunk is the basic unit of content, and a chunk addressing scheme says how to name chunks and describe which ones a peer has. All peers in a swarm MUST use the same scheme.

Chunk ranges are a start and end chunk ID, each a 32-bit or 64-bit unsigned integer. Every peer MUST support this scheme. Byte ranges use 64-bit byte offsets and are optional.

Bin numbers are a PPSPP novelty, also optional. A balanced binary tree is built over the chunks. Leaves get the numbers I*2 for chunk index I, and each parent gets (binL + binR) / 2. A single integer then names any binary interval of chunks, which reduces per-peer state and the space needed on the wire. For example, with eight chunks, bin 7 is the whole interval, bin 3 covers chunks C0 to C3, and bin 2 is chunk C1.

A HAVE must name the biggest complete interval the receiver now holds that includes the new chunks. As a result every chunk is acknowledged a logarithmic number of times, which makes up for unreliable transport.
sections.eli5: Instead of listing every piece you have, you use a numbering trick so one number can mean a whole run of pieces, like saying "the first half of the book".

sections.title: Integrity and Live Streaming
sections.content:
For static content PPSPP uses a Merkle hash tree. Each chunk is hashed, hashes are paired and hashed up the tree, and the top is the root hash, which also serves as the swarm ID. A receiver that trusts the root hash checks any chunk using the hashes of the chunk's sibling and its "uncles", recalculating the root. Senders can skip hashes the receiver must already know. In the RFC's example, a simple progressive download of the 7-chunk tree sends 7 hashes rather than all 16 in the tree.

The atomic datagram principle says each datagram should be processable alone, so a chunk's hashes should go in the same datagram as the chunk. Otherwise the INTEGRITY messages go first. Using this scheme over the Internet is required, and the RFC explains that BitTorrent-style hash lists would force a large download before playback can start.

For live streams the tree keeps growing, so the swarm ID is a public key. Two methods exist. Sign All signs every chunk and is optional. Unified Merkle Tree is mandatory to implement and signs only the "munro" hash of each new subtree of NCHUNKS_PER_SIG chunks, a power of 2 greater than 1. That means one signature check per group of chunks, at the cost of more latency. Peers announce their rightmost signed munro hash so that a new viewer can securely tune in. A discarding peer sets the Live Discard Window option so others know which old chunks are gone. After a broadcast ends, the stable tree and final root hash let the recording be served as on-demand content.
sections.eli5: Each piece gets a fingerprint, and fingerprints are combined into one master fingerprint of the whole video. For a live show that never ends, the broadcaster signs a note for each batch of pieces so you can trust them.

sections.title: Protocol Options and UDP
sections.content:
The HANDSHAKE carries a list of protocol options, each an 8-bit code and usually an 8-bit value. The list MUST be sorted by code and end with the End Option (code 255). Version must come first. The options cover the swarm ID, integrity method, Merkle hash function (SHA-256 is the default, and SHA-1 and SHA-256 MUST be supported), live signature algorithm (the default is ECDSAP256SHA256), chunk addressing method (the default is 32-bit chunk ranges), live discard window, supported messages and chunk size.

Implementations MUST use UDP and MUST use LEDBAT for congestion control. LEDBAT is delay-based and backs off early, which lets a peer keep seeding after playback without disturbing the user's other traffic. The RECOMMENDED chunk size is a fixed 1024 bytes, which fits in a single IP packet over Ethernet with 1500-byte frames. A chunk and its integrity messages should fit in one datagram. The six IANA registries for message types, options, versions, integrity methods, hash functions and addressing methods use the IETF Review policy for unassigned values.
sections.eli5: When two peers meet they swap a short form listing the settings they use. Everything runs on a polite, gentle sending style that backs off when the network is busy.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC admits that privacy is unlikely, since a user exposes their IP address to peers. It analyses three denial-of-service attacks on the handshake: amplification (using a peer to flood a victim), state flooding, and spoofed messages that disrupt a particular peer. The random channel IDs and the rule that no heavy payload is sent before the third datagram provide a return routability check against the first and third. The second is only partly addressed: a handshake with state allocation is a bit vulnerable, so a peer that is still interested MUST respond immediately to the second datagram. The RFC chose this faster handshake over the SCTP style so that users see video sooner.

Peer exchange can enable amplification and Eclipse attacks, where malicious peers try to isolate a victim, for instance the live injector. Defences include membership certificates, for example signed by a tracker acting as certificate authority, and keeping some connections to peers whose addresses came from a trusted tracker. Confidentiality is left to content publishers (encrypting content, or using Closed Swarms, DTLS or IPsec). The document also lists per-message limits to contain damage from bad or broken peers.
sections.eli5: Because many strangers join, the rules include ways to make sure a peer is really who it says, and ways to stop someone from tricking you into talking only to bad actors.

messages.label: channel 0 + HANDSHAKE(chanP)
messages.note: Swarm ID in the options. Minor payload only, no heavy payload.

messages.label: chanP + HANDSHAKE(chanQ)
messages.note: Echoing chanP proves Q really responds. Minor payload only.

messages.label: chanQ + HAVE + DATA
messages.note: Heavy payload is now allowed. Q learns P really received its reply.

items.label: HANDSHAKE
items.desc: Opens or closes a channel and carries protocol options.

items.label: DATA
items.desc: A chunk, with its chunk specification and a timestamp.

items.label: ACK
items.desc: Acknowledges received chunks with a one-way delay sample.

items.label: HAVE
items.desc: States which verified chunks the sender holds.

items.label: INTEGRITY
items.desc: A hash needed to verify a chunk.

items.label: PEX_REQ
items.desc: Asks a peer for peer addresses.

items.label: SIGNED_INTEGRITY
